summary:
Acts is the sequel to the Gospel of Luke — both books open with a dedication to the same man, Theophilus — and it is the only narrative history of the early church in the New Testament. It picks up where the gospel left off: the risen Jesus spends forty days with his disciples, then ascends into heaven with a promise: "You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth." That sentence is the outline of the entire book. Acts traces the growth of a small band of Galilean followers into a movement that reaches Rome itself within a single generation.

The first chapters center on Peter and the church in Jerusalem. Pentecost is the starting point: the Holy Spirit descends with a sound like rushing wind and tongues like flames of fire, the disciples speak in languages they have never learned, and Peter preaches to a crowd of festival pilgrims from across the known world. About three thousand people believe in a single day. The new community shares its possessions and breaks bread together, but not without conflict: Ananias and Sapphira drop dead for lying about their giving, and the apostles are arrested, flogged, and ordered to stop preaching. Their answer: "We must obey God rather than men." Stephen, on trial before the council for his preaching, looks up and says, "I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God" — and is dragged out and stoned, the first of Jesus' followers killed for the message, while the witnesses lay their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul.

The stoning touches off a persecution that scatters the believers — and the scattering spreads the message along exactly the route Jesus had named. Philip preaches in Samaria and then explains the scroll of Isaiah to an Ethiopian royal official on a desert road. Peter, shown a vision of a sheet filled with animals he has always considered unclean, enters the house of a Roman centurion named Cornelius and watches the Holy Spirit fall on the whole Gentile household: "I now truly understand that God does not show favoritism, but welcomes those from every nation who fear Him and do what is right." And in Antioch, where the scattered believers begin preaching to Greeks in large numbers, the movement acquires its lasting name: "The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch."

Threaded through these chapters is the event Acts retells three times (chapters 9, 22, and 26): Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee hunting down believers, is blinded by a light on the road to Damascus and hears a voice — "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?" The persecutor becomes the preacher. From chapter 13 on, the spotlight is on Paul's missionary journeys — traditionally counted as three — through Cyprus, Asia Minor, and Greece. He plants churches in Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth, and Ephesus; debates philosophers in Athens, taking as his opening text an altar inscribed TO AN UNKNOWN GOD; is stoned and left for dead at Lystra, then gets up and walks back into the city. In Thessalonica the charge against the missionaries is that "these men who have turned the world upside down have now come here." Partway through the journeys the narration quietly shifts from "they" to "we" — the traditional inference is that the author himself joined Paul's traveling party.

All these Gentile conversions force a question: must non-Jewish believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses? The Jerusalem Council of chapter 15 settles it. Peter points back to what happened in Cornelius's house; James quotes the prophet Amos to show that God had always promised to include the nations; and the council's letter asks Gentile converts to abstain from a short list of practices rather than take on the whole law. Peter's words carry the weight of the decision: "we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are."

Paul comes to Rome as a prisoner. Seized in the temple in Jerusalem and held for two years in Caesarea while governors stall, he finally exercises his right as a Roman citizen: "I appeal to Caesar!" The voyage is a disaster survived — a two-week storm, shipwreck off Malta, a viper that fastens onto his hand while the islanders wait for him to drop dead. The book ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome for two full years, welcoming everyone who comes to him: "Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ." His trial before Caesar is never narrated. Luke leaves Paul where the promise of the first chapter has carried him — bearing witness in the capital of the empire — and the book's last word in Greek is an adverb meaning "unhindered."
